scenes.script_line: Most of us are fairly easy to understand when things are going well. The more interesting question is: what happens to you when things are not going well? When plans change. When you feel ignored. When someone disagrees with you. When work becomes repetitive. When you feel disconnected from the team. Or when you feel like you are not growing. Pressure often reveals which human needs matter most to us. And when one of those needs feels threatened, our behavior can change quickly. The goal is not to stop having needs. The goal is to recognize what is happening inside us before we react automatic
scenes.visual_direction: Calm workplace scenes shifting into changing plans, disagreement, deadlines, repeated tasks, or uncertainty.

scenes.script_line: If certainty is important to you, change can feel uncomfortable. A new process. A different schedule. Unexpected information. A plan that suddenly changes. Under pressure, your first reaction might be: "Why are we changing this?" You may become more rigid. More controlling. Or more focused on getting everything back to the way it was. The healthier question is: "What do I know, what do I not know, and what can I do next?" Certainty does not have to come from everything staying the same. It can come from preparation, communication, skill, and your confidence that you can adapt.
scenes.visual_direction: Schedule changes, new instructions, employee initially frustrated, then reviewing information and adapting.

scenes.script_line: If variety is one of your stronger needs, pressure can show up differently. Routine may begin to feel frustrating. You may want to change things quickly. Start something new. Jump between tasks. Or solve the problem by doing something completely different. Variety can make you creative and flexible. But under pressure, it can also pull you away from consistency. Ask yourself: "Do we actually need a change, or do I just need stimulation?" Sometimes the best response is innovation. Sometimes the best response is simply finishing what you started.
scenes.visual_direction: Employee jumping between tasks or ideas, then slowing down, prioritizing, and completing one thing.

scenes.script_line: If connection matters deeply to you, conflict can feel particularly uncomfortable. You may worry that someone is upset with you. You may avoid saying what needs to be said. You may agree when you actually disagree. Or you may take someone’s tone more personally than they intended. The desire for connection is healthy. But healthy connection is not the same as keeping everyone happy. Sometimes the strongest relationships require honesty. Ask: "Am I protecting the relationship, or am I avoiding discomfort?" Trust grows when people can communicate clearly, respectfully, and honestly.

scenes.script_line: If growth is a major driver for you, you may become frustrated when you feel stuck. Maybe the work feels repetitive. Maybe you are not learning as quickly as you want. Maybe you are doing something you already know how to do. Under pressure, you may become impatient. Disengaged. Or decide that there is nothing left to learn. But growth is not always given to us through a new task. Sometimes growth comes from going deeper. Doing something with greater skill. Improving quality. Becoming more efficient. Learning to communicate better. Or mastering something you previously only knew how to do adeq

scenes.script_line: Contribution can also have an unhealthy side. If helping others is very important to you, you may start taking on everything. Fixing problems that belong to someone else. Always saying yes. Doing other people’s work because it feels easier than allowing them to learn. You may have good intentions. But over-contributing can create dependency, frustration, and exhaustion. Sometimes contribution means helping. Sometimes contribution means teaching. And sometimes contribution means allowing another person to take responsibility. Ask: "Am I truly helping, or am I taking over?"
scenes.visual_direction: Employee taking on multiple colleagues tasks, then shifting to coaching, explaining, and allowing someone else to complete the work.

scenes.script_line: The most useful skill here is simple: pause before you react. When you notice yourself becoming frustrated, defensive, controlling, distracted, withdrawn, or overwhelmed, ask: "Which need am I trying to meet right now?" Then ask: "Is the way I am meeting it helping me?" That small pause creates choice. Instead of reacting automatically, you can respond intentionally. Maybe you need more information. Maybe you need a challenge. Maybe you need to let go of being right. Maybe you need to have an honest conversation. Maybe you need to find a new opportunity to learn. Or maybe you need to stop taki

scenes.script_line: Think about the last time you felt frustrated or under pressure at work. What happened? And then ask yourself: which human need felt threatened? Was it certainty? Variety? Significance? Connection? Growth? Contribution? Then ask: how did I respond? And what might a healthier response have looked like? The more you recognize your patterns, the less those patterns control you. Pressure will happen. Change will happen. Difficult conversations will happen. What matters is becoming better at choosing how you respond.
